title: Polaris Sector
text: One more "unpaused turn" syndrome approved. Really nice 4X SciFi game, very snappy, robust mechanics, super fun and challenging tactical fleet combat (in realtime pausable, super slow mode possible,...). I prefer turn based combat usually, but the way you can slow down the fight to a crawl is good enough for me. Once you get the rythm, the game flows naturally, there are no restrictions: - conquer as many star systems as you want/need. - create as many fleets as you want with as many ships inside as you want. - wage wars everywhere at the same time if it's your call. (every fights will be resolve by you, one at a time, no stress) - Even the research tree progresses on multiple technological domains at the same time. (very clever and logical) This game is Pure Freedom, no obnoxious limiting mechanics that you could endure in many others 4X games. Big up for the guys who have written the races' lore, you made me laughing out loud so hard ! ;-)

title: Polaris Sector
text: This game is really fun and good. I am enjoying myself a lot. I love the slow buildup until you unlock more and more (more tech, more systems, more ship designs). It's a very nice pace, though definitely not for those who are in a rush (although, I guess if so you can set colonies to automanage any of 8 or so preset builds (and you can even create custom builds for the automanager to follow!) and play with high time acceleration). But as I like to micromanage everything that just feels great too. There are many different types of galaxies and the differences in how you play and expand are rather large between a number of those. The galaxy creation has many settings to tailor stuff to your liking, and you can even set things like whether or not colonization ships get consumed on use (or just lose their colonists) and whether or not you can recover destroyed/disabled fighter craft after a battle. You can handle battles yourself as well, which imo is a huge bonus (though not ground battles, just space ones, but that's fine imo). I easily recommend this!

title: Polaris Sector
text: Let me say first off that I have only played for four hours so far which isn't long enough for an in depth review, it is long enough however for a first impressions and so far those impressions are not good.  I will also say that when it comes to 4x games I am an empire builder.  I strategize and try to see the big picture.  In space 4x I build two or three poweful battle fleets and station them where they can get to probable trouble spots in a reasonable and timely manner.  Polaris sector while appearing to offer similar on the surface actually falls flat once that surface has been penetrated and you get to the soft and not so juicy bits underneath.  You would think that with a map size of 900 stars it would be awhile before you needed to deal with the other major factions, but no.  The game sticks them fairly close so you will start to bump up against them within the first hour of play which makes the map feel smaller than it is, a feeling that is compounded by the stars themselves being quite close to each other and by the pirates that pop up seemingly out of nowhere to harass your worlds and shipping, seriously, turn these off as they are way too common. The developers really should have looked at another game in the Matrix stable ( Distant Worlds ) and taken a few hints.  Polaris sector has fallen squarely into that old and tired 4x land grab.  Find colonisable world / grab it before the Ai does / try to close off choke points and build huge defences and fleets because you know what's coming.  It's been done to death and it's boring.  You will also find that after a couple of hours the game will auto-pause with nausiating regularity ( every few seconds ) that has you delving into the settings to turn most of it off, which then results in you missing information if the game speed is turned up ( something that you need to do in order to get anywhere ). One of the main innovations ( according to the developer ) is the research system that boasts no research trees.  Yes there are, they are just displayed differently and research usually devolves into choosing which tech you want next, prioritising it and letting the game get on with churning it out.  Having said that the techs appear many and diverse but with the way the larger game is designed you will find yourself researching the military techs early on so that your ships are not completely outgunned, which is another similarity to many 4x games out there.  Again, perhaps they should have taken a look at Distant Worlds in which techs are split into three different categories allowing for more civilian techs to be researched alongside the military ones.  The ship designer is a variation on a theme first implemented in another 4x game that shall remain nameless but Polaris sector does it better and some interesting combinations can be produced.  I created a fleet of stealth / assassin ships that waited at a choke point for any unsuspecting enemy vessels to wander by.  The pirates got a taste of their own medicine with that lot. As I said, I have not played long enough for a full review and I will update this when I have a few more hours under my belt.  Hopefully the game will get better as I delve deeper into it but first impressions matter and these have been mine. Now almost 8 hours in and I'm honestly bored to tears.  I was hoping that the game would blossom and show it's complexity as I got further into it but no, there really is none.  Polaris Sector is one of the most shallow space 4x games that I have ever played and I have played a few of them.  The couple of wafer thin strategic elements that the game brings to the table, the created bottlenecks and the combat have issues of their own and add nothing to the gameplay which is bland and uninspired.  The bottlenecks are created because of the use of warp lanes.  i know why the developers use them, it's to prevent both the player and the Ai from attacking out of nowhere ( mainly the player ) but we are in 2016 here and there are better ways of handling that particular problem.  as it is it just adds one more thing that takes away the immersion and places you on a linear road rather than the expanse of space.  The combat system was quaint for the first few outings but quickly became tiresome and tedious, leaving me to auto-resolve or to tell my fleets to do their own thing, which invariably means frontal assault and tactics be damned.  Simply look at the red / green bar and if you have more than they do then auto-resolve it, you will win. Matrix produce some decent strategy games if you can get past the decades old graphics but sadly this isn't one of them.  I have clicked 'close and continue' so many %$£^$%£ times in the past few hours while the game pretty much played itself that my index finger has developed a twitch.  If you really must have this in your library then wait for a steam sale.

title: Polaris Sector
text: This is not a bad game. What is bad is what you get for the price. Before release Slitherine games said they had a "system" for setting price on games, and they were an expert because of all the games they have released. They said if game was too cheap people would not take it serious. I almost laughed at this. I personally refunded the game because I felt it was too much money, and certainly would have kept it had the price been more reasonable for what is offered. So what is offered? Well basically a streamlined combat focused 4x. It has all the elements of a 4x, but simplified. There is still a learning curve, but not a steep one. Combat is where this game shines the best, with a half decent combat viewer and some tactical choices that can be made during battles. I also personally enjoy the fuel system for ships, though last I knew the AI ignored this system (free fuel), so it was only a restriction on the player, which is a bummer. I enjoy doing a lot of the aspects of 4x's that were streamlined in this game. (meaning I dont want them simplified like this game does) Its kinda hard to explain unless you watch a video of gameplay. I hate to bring it into this review, but (almost) everything this game does, Stellaris does 4x better... pun intended. Though to be fair Stellaris has more people working on it, and Stellaris is not perfect either, but Polaris Sector is missing so much in comparison, I will not even bother to compare the 2 games, except to say that they are the same price, which should say something about the price of Polaris Sector. One good thing to mention, although I have not been active on the forums recently, is that the developer was very responsive and friendly last time I was lurking about. I also did not experience any bugs while playing the game. Overall it is a good streamlined 4x title but priced too high. I would wait for a sale to pick it up. If the price was 20 bucks or less, this game would still be in my library.

title: Polaris Sector
text: One word... Fantasic, absolutely fantastic! Ok, that's 2 words. In all seriousness though, Polaris Sector does something that no other Space 4X game has done in years. It simplifies the rubbish often found in 4X games, and also adds a new twist on the genre's often seen staples. My favourite Real Time 4X (and overall PC title) game has always been Imperium Galactica 2. Polaris Sector comes a close 2nd. Whilst it may not have an implemented storyline or the polish of IG2. It's unique enough to hold its own ground in a very solid manner. The UI is very well implemented as not to confuse the mechanics and the general gameplay is easy enough to follow without having to concern yourself with a Distant Worlds: Universe kind of depth. Some may be turned off with the slow burn of the game, as depending on how many races you place into the game and the number of systems, a single game can take many many hours. But since this game does have 9 races, as well as the ability to customise these races, plus a number of galaxy types.. With the added bonus of random generation, this game's replay value can be considered immense, and this is well worth the asking price! All in all, as a verteran of the 4X genre, this is a game I could highly recommend. Whilst it could likely do with more random encounters and some elements of a storyline to increase the lore of the entire universe further. It certainly wins my personal reccomendation.

title: Polaris Sector
text: I'm going to preface my review by saying that there are some things that I like about this game.  However, there are more things that I dislike about it. Pros: 1.  The starmap is quite beautiful and can be expansive.  It is also easy to understand at a glance. 2.  The building automation AI for the worlds is pretty good.  I just wish there were more options to go with or a popup when a planet is done building with the automation. 3.  The tech tree is vast and there is a lot to play with.  However, see "Cons" for further information. Cons: 1.  The races are not that unique.  They feel fairly cookie-cutter due to easily customizing them when starting a game.  Truthfully, you could choose one race and give it all of the bonuses of another race. 2.  The tech tree might be vast, but it's linear and extremely hard to really plan long-term as there is no real tree to look at.  It's linear in the fact that techs will be learned in the exact same order in every game you play unless you play with the sliders to research different things faster.  However, techs are still in the same line.  The tech tree is also almost impossible to look at ingame to see what to focus on what to get to a specific tech.  The devs provided a website with all the possible techs, but it's also difficult to navigate and plan with as well. 3.  Here is the biggest problem with this game:  Racial ship balance.  Certain races have pathetically bad ships due to having either vastly lower number of slots, or having much higher build costs, or both.  Terrans are an example of the "both" category.  It's a really bad game design that needs to be fixed for this game really to have any long-lasting appeal and replayability. 4.  And, finally, the AI is truly blood-thirsty.  Even peaceful races see military-weak races as targets for conquest.

title: Poly Bridge
text: If there was a middle option between recommending and not recommending the game, I would gladly take it. On the one hand I did enjoy building bridges, finding solution to specific locations and requirements. But on the other hand, I felt a little bit cheated and lied to, thinking as I did that I would have to build sensible bridges for sensible situations, using proper planning and logic. But then I found myself building not just bridges, but also ridiculous ramps and swings, building death-defying contraptions to get a bus across as if it were a non valuable crate that could risk being destroyed, building Rube Goldberg machines of getting motorized vehicles from point A to point B that made no engineering sense but just fit the materials and budget I was allowed. The most infuriating was that it often felt like moving a connecting point a single pixel to the side could be the difference between utter failure and glorious success. As a consequence I ended up just moving pixels about until it finally worked, which is not how I normally like to proceed. Writing all of this, I do wonder why I'm even pressing the recommend button instead of the other one, but I still had some fun building some of the less ludicrous bridges in the less implausible situations. When all is said and done I guess this is a game to enjoy not any longer than it is actually enjoyable.

title: Poly Bridge
text: Simply put, this is a janky game that requires you to obsess over where you put every last poly of the bridge.  There's no real puzzle element to it where you go, "of course, that makes sense." No your solution will probably make sense from the start, it's simply that you aren't putting the polys in the exact right position to support your bridges. Furthermore, there's never a tutorial that tells you, "you should use a suspension bridge in this situation or an arch in this other situation".  It's just, "give it a try and figure it out yourself." The tutorial boils down to an instruction manual.  It tells you a few odd techniques you wouldn't think of on your own and how all the tools work.  However, what I want is a little more depth there.  Give me some more detailed information.  For example, when should I use ropes instead of steel?  Is there an iron-clad rule about their use? There are even a few tricks I had to learn on youtube which weren't included in the manual at all.  The ability to tie supports together with rope instead of wood/steel for one. It would be nice for example if you told us what supports to improve first and under which circumstances.  For example, let's say that road section B is breaking and it currently has wood supports.  Should I upgrade them to steel first? Reinforce the road? Change to ropes? Finally, for anyone else having trouble with the hydraulics.  When you seperate a poly for a hydraulic bridge, the side indicated on the split is not indicative of which side of the split you are dealing with.  It's really confusing as all hell and I spent a full hour figuring out that the red square side of the split is ALWAYS the land mass, even when it's on the opposite side of the land mass.

title: Portal Stories: Mel
text: Get this game if you even remotely like Portal or Portal 2. It is an awesome production made by people who not only love the Portal games, but understand what made them such gems. The test chambers(puzzles) in this game are some of the finest I have seen and equally match the quality of the original games. The test chambers in the game, however, are much harder than those found in Portal 1 or 2. This is not necessarily a bad thing, but be warned: This game does not hold your hand and difficult puzzles appear quite early in the game. It is assumed you have played both Portal and Portal 2 and they utilize not only the skills you learned in those games, but innovate in ways that require you to think in new ways. Everything, however, does makes sense and the puzzles have logical solutions. I played and beat the entire game and I only found one solution that I considered "cheap". It involved using the laser bridges to lift a box off a switch, something I did not know could happen. That is minor nitpicking, though. The vast majority of the puzzles are mind-bending, logical, and extremely satisfying to play. I spent 45 minutes solving one with my wife and even though we made minimal progress, we both agreed that we enjoyed puzzling through the particular chamber we were on. The final puzzle, a timed battle similar to the one in Portal 1, is a total pain an is an unfortunate mark against the game. You are required to use the turrets to shoot things and placing turrets is actually quite difficult. They tip over too easy, self-destruct, and you can hardly control your rage when you are trying to do the right thing and can not. Anyway, overall, this game deserves huge marks. Valve should hire the individuals that made this game to devise a genuine Portal 3, though this game almost serves as Portal 3 already. It's puzzles are top notch, it's story is quite captivating, the voice acting is excellent, and the overall production values are amazing. Anyone who likes Portal even a little should get this game and enjoy it to the fullest. 9/10 - nearly perfect!

title: Pox Nora
text: I tried writing a review of this game before, but back then I didn't think I had given this game a fair shake. First off, this game is not a card game, its essentially a strategy board game similar to... well, I don't know of many that are still played in this day and age so I'll just go with classics such as Heroscape and Necromunda. (You don't even know what those are do you) You play by assembling your battlegroup from runes (cards that essentially work as model figures) and supporting them with spells and equipment. As far as these types of games go, Pox Nora is deep, and has had years to develop its rune catalog. There are eight factions, of which a battlegroup can be composed of at most 2. Runes have rarity and differing efficiency values, but all are useful in some way or another. That being said, discovering this usefulness can be tricky as the game is not straightforward and figuring it all out is essentially trial and error. There is a tutorial, but it's terrible, and the steam interface could use some improvement. Is the game P2W? No, not anymore. It used to be, which is when I first started writing this review some time ago when the gold income was paltry and winning battles didn't give out free runes (cards. You know what? I'm just going to call them cards) Now, its possible to get really good cards for free without ever having to play another player, which is a good thing because, quite frankly, I find the community could try a little harder to accomadate newer players. It will still take lots of games and lots of times to put together your own battlegroup, but the game has many free battlegroups you can play while collecting your set, and no, they don't suck. The graphics are a bit dated, but if you don't mind that, then their's no reason to talk about it. If you do mind it, your either going to look past it, or not. Either way, they are what they are. To sum up, if you like card games and board games, and don't mind dated graphics or figuring things out by yourself, give Pox Nora a shot. The game is improving with time now that its under a new developer, but it still has a long way to go to compete with powerhouses such as MTG or Hearthstone.

title: Pox Nora
text: Edit: Based on the game many years ago, so some of this changed since then. PoxNora has a special place in my heart. I played it for hundreds of hours prior to steam when the game was still young and they had just changed the game to remove all random numbers (no "hit chance" or "dice rolls" - pure strategy without random numbers). Back then it was a revelation and since then most other strategy games I play ended up being disappointing when I compare them to PoxNora. Why did I quit and don't recommend it? It's a digital trading card game. You needed to invest significant money and trading to get a competitive deck. There were limited edition cards that were being sold for several hundred dollar. Then suddenly previously limited cards were suddenly sold on a "first come" basis without a warning, increasing in price the more frequently they were bought. Powerful legacy cards that rarely saw action got picked up for a dollar or two -- yet the price jumped very high within a day and most people missed out making the matches very unbalanced suddenly. Then the new expansions kept adding insane epic cards (powercreep...), while completely devaluing other cards. In the end I had to sell my cards because I had spend significant cash on them and the company kept devaluing them with each update. Moral of the story: There is a reason classic trading card games are being replaced by living card games (fixed expansions instead of booster packs) because people rightfully think trading card games are robbing their wallet. A game where you buy digital cards for insane costs yet the company only changes a database entry and at any point in time can make your investment worthless? Great idea. Thumbs down.
